title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

title: Follow the Money: The State and the Architecture of Union Funding
abstract: ABSTRACT Trade unions need money to sustain the staff, infrastructure and activities on which all forms of union power depend, yet the financial dimensions of unions and their power have been largely overlooked in the comparative study of industrial relations. This article addresses the gap by using unions’ financial means as a revealing lens for understanding the role of the state in shaping union power. The comparison distinguished two ideal‐typical logics of state action behind union funding. Under indirect action, the state enables unions to convert membership into income, producing a tight coupling between union funds and organisational power. Under direct action, the state channels funds to unions on the basis of their recognised societal roles, decoupling income from membership. Systematised during the early decades of the twentieth century, these two action paths present fundamental transformations through liberalisation, leading to the financialisation and politicisation of union funding. By analysing the structures and changes in unions’ financial sustainability, this framework reveals the state's constitutive role in shaping and transforming union power.

title: Union Membership and Native-Immigrant Labour Market Gaps
authors: Samuel Dodini; Alexander Willén; Julia Li Zhu
abstract: Abstract We estimate the causal effects of union membership on labour market outcomes for natives and immigrants, exploiting quasi-experimental variation from large increases in Norway’s tax deduction for union dues. Union membership raises earnings and improves employment protection for native workers, while the private returns for non-Western immigrants are substantially smaller and often close to zero. Complementary survey evidence suggests that this gap is not explained by differences in information, preferences, or engagement with unions: immigrants receive similar information when joining, report similar preferences over job amenities, and are more likely than natives to seek union assistance. Instead, the combined administrative and survey evidence is consistent with differences in union-side behaviour. Immigrants report lower satisfaction after contacting unions for support and are more likely to believe that native workers and those with strong local networks receive greater benefits from membership. The impact is most pronounced in concentrated labour markets, indicating that relying on unions to address monopsony-based market failures may unintentionally amplify group inequalities.

From Gender Antagonism to Inclusive Solidarity? Trade Union Membership and Attitudes Toward Women's Employment
abstract: ABSTRACT Why and to what extent do union members differ from non‐members in attitudes toward women's employment? This study argues that a masculinized conception of work has historically underpinned gender antagonism in trade unionism, and that the rise of right‐wing populism may have hindered recent progress toward gender equality among union members. Analyzing the European Values Study data, I find that union members hold more egalitarian attitudes toward women's employment than non‐members on average. This relationship further varies across individual and institutional characteristics. After the financial crisis, however, the positive association has weakened particularly in countries where right‐wing populism is influential.
journal: Industrial Relations A Journal of Economy and Society

title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data
abstract: Abstract We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

title: Sustainable Solidarity: Navigating Network and Bureaucracy to Resist Precarity
abstract: The transition to electric vehicles is reshaping labor markets as production expands within supplier networks. This transformation has deepened inequalities between core workers, protected by stable employment and collective agreements, and peripheral workers facing growing precarity. This study examines the Module-Suppliers Alliance (MSA) in South Korea’s automobile sector, where subcontracted workers adopted a network-based strategy to improve wages and employment security. The findings show that while network-based organizing enabled rapid mobilization and broad participation during the organizing phase, it proved less effective during bargaining as divergent interests and coordination challenges emerged. Tracing the MSA’s evolving collaboration with the Korean Metal Workers’ Union (KMWU), the study demonstrates how workers alternate between network-based organizing and bureaucratic (hierarchical) coordination across successive phases of struggle, with such coordination introduced during bargaining to complement network-based forms of organization. The author argues that this process of bureaucratic layering can sustain worker solidarity under conditions of precarity.

title: The Hidden Effects of Company Strikes: Workers Made Idle in UK Engineering and Metalworking From 1920 to 1970
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines a neglected aspect of industrial relations: workplace disputes in which workers are incidentally made idle because of strike actions of others. These spillover effects have received little systematic attention despite potentially accounting for a substantial share of the employment consequences of industrial conflict. The analysis uses a comprehensive dataset of company strikes compiled by the UK Engineering Employers' Federation (EEF) between 1920 and 1970, recording both workers directly involved in disputes and non‐striking employees made idle. During the interwar and wartime periods, relatively few workers were made idle compared with those directly on strike. In contrast, the post‐war period saw a substantial rise in the likelihood and scale of incidental idleness. By the late 1960s, the number of EEF workers made idle by strikes nearly matched the hundreds of thousands on strike. Incidental idleness was especially likely when strikes were caused by non‐pay disputes, most notably those involving a demarcation disagreement about how workers from different unions or with different trades were assigned to tasks in the plant. These findings highlight wider employment consequences of industrial conflict, especially where there are production interdependencies.

title: The Evolution of Hours Worked and the Gender Wage Gap: Evidence From Four Countries
authors: Daniele Checchi; Daniel Kreisman; Cecilia García-Peñalosa
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the contribution of the intensive margin of labor supply (hours worked above zero) to the gender wage gap over a long time‐horizon across four high‐income economies: France, Germany, the UK, and the US. We do so by bridging a recent literature on gender differences in high‐paying, high‐hour jobs with traditional wage gap decomposition methods. We first build a model in which firms offer two wage contracts—one that pays a fixed wage but allows workers to choose their preferred number of hours up to “full time,” and a second in which wages are determined by imperfectly observable productivity and can require working more than standard hours. The former includes part‐ and full‐time work, while the latter requires workers to supply long hours but allows them to earn a higher remuneration. We then decompose the hourly wage gap separately for part‐, full‐, and overtime workers to observe the relative contribution of sorting and remuneration across these “hours regimes” over time and across countries. We show that while female employment in overtime work has increased and the gender wage gap has decreased in most countries and hours regimes, this was not driven by increasing selection on observables but rather by a decline over time of the unexplained component of the wage gap—a pattern that holds for most countries and hours regimes. We conclude by considering the contribution of the institutional framework (unions, labor market flexibility, parental leaves) to these cross‐country differences.

title: Who Benefits From Right‐to‐Disconnect Legislation in Europe? Cross‐National and Gendered Effects on Employee Wellbeing
abstract: ABSTRACT The effectiveness of labour regulation depends not only on the formal articulation of rights, but on the institutional arrangements through which those rights are enforced and distributed across workers. This is particularly salient for regulations governing working time and employee availability, where outcomes are shaped by power relations in the workplace and persistent gendered divisions of paid and unpaid labour. The introduction of right‐to‐disconnect (R2D) legislation in several European countries provides a valuable opportunity to examine how procedural labour rights operate across different industrial relations systems and how they generate gender‐differentiated outcomes. Rather than constituting a single policy model, R2D provisions vary substantially in their reliance on collective bargaining, firm‐level discretion and individual characteristics. Using data from the European Social Survey between 2010 and 2022 and exploiting the staggered introduction of R2D policies in France, Belgium, Spain, Ireland and Portugal, this study estimates effects on subjective wellbeing among employees in teleworkable occupations. Applying a dynamic difference‐in‐differences approach, the analysis identifies modest average improvements in wellbeing in countries where R2D provisions are embedded within stronger industrial relations systems. Gendered analyses show that these benefits accrue more consistently to men than to women, highlighting how digital labour regulation may interact with unequal distributions of paid and unpaid work.

title: AI and Stress
abstract: ABSTRACT Given the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) tools at work, understanding their health implications is critically important. We use rich survey data from Finland and apply propensity score matching that accounts for observable differences between regular AI users and non‐users to estimate the relationship between reported AI usage at work and workers’ reported stress. Regular AI use is associated with a 4.4 percentage point higher probability of reporting stress, equivalent to a 25.6% increase relative to baseline. Comparing two competing explanations, we find that this pattern is more consistent with heavier work demands than with concerns about job loss: AI use is associated with more unpaid work outside working hours and, less precisely, with intense work absorption, but not with job insecurity. Exploratory subgroup estimates are larger and individually significant for men, non‐supervisors, unionized workers and employees in medium‐sized workplaces, although the differences across subgroups are not statistically significant.

title: Occupational Preferences Heterogeneity in Labor Supply: Evidence from the PSID
abstract: Empirical research generally finds that wage fluctuations lead to only modest adjustments in hours worked. However, individuals experiencing economic hardship often increase their labor supply when wages decline, exhibiting negative labor supply elasticity, a phenomenon documented in both less industrialized economies and certain high-income countries. Using micro-level data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) spanning 1968 to 2017, this study investigates heterogeneity in labor supply elasticity across occupations and industries, with particular attention to the influence of work-environment characteristics and non-pecuniary job attributes. Our findings reveal substantial variation in Frisch elasticity that is systematically associated with occupational characteristics and individual work preferences. Workers in construction, extraction, production, and transportation occupations display relatively high labor supply elasticity, indicating greater responsiveness to wage fluctuations and a stronger propensity to substitute leisure for labor. In contrast, individuals employed in the arts, sports, and social services exhibit lower elasticity estimates, consistent with the hypothesis that these occupations provide higher intrinsic satisfaction or other non-pecuniary returns, thereby reducing sensitivity to wage changes. We further observe cross-state variation in Frisch elasticities that reflect underlying institutional differences in labor market regulation, unionization, and employment protection. Overall, the evidence highlights the importance of occupational heterogeneity and non-pecuniary job characteristics in shaping labor supply behavior at the intensive margin. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying labor supply responsiveness and underscore the need to account for non-monetary job attributes when evaluating labor market dynamics.
